title: SEC-Big Ten Schedule Deal Looms as CFP Expands to 24 Teams, Says Joel Klatt
body:
The College Football Playoff is slated to grow from its current 12‑team format to a 24‑team field beginning with the 2027 season, and the change could reshape the power dynamics of the sport’s two most lucrative conferences. Fox analyst Joel Klatt warned that the expansion will likely prompt the SEC and the Big Ten to negotiate a new scheduling agreement, a move that could alter traditional rivalries, revenue streams, and the competitive balance of college football for years to come.

Klatt’s comments come amid growing pressure from conference commissioners, university presidents, and television partners who have long argued that the existing playoff structure limits access for deserving programs while inflating the stakes of conference championship games. By doubling the number of playoff participants, the NCAA hopes to address criticism that the current format favors a handful of elite programs and leaves too many high‑performing teams on the outside. However, a larger field also means more games, more travel, and a longer season, which could strain already packed conference schedules.

The SEC and Big Ten, which together command roughly half of the sport’s television revenue, have historically set their own calendars well in advance, often arranging non‑conference matchups years ahead. With a 24‑team playoff, the number of games required to determine a champion will increase, potentially creating conflicts with existing conference commitments. Klatt predicts that the two leagues will look to synchronize their schedules to ensure that member schools can accommodate the extended postseason without sacrificing marquee non‑conference games that attract national audiences and lucrative sponsorships.

A coordinated schedule could take several forms. One possibility is a “flex” window later in the season where both conferences agree to limit non‑conference contests, allowing teams to preserve health and preparation time for the expanded playoff. Another scenario involves a joint agreement to rotate cross‑conference matchups, preserving historic rivalries such as Michigan‑Ohio State and Alabama‑Georgia while also introducing new inter‑conference series that could boost viewership. The financial incentive is significant: a larger playoff promises higher advertising revenue and a bigger share of the television rights pie, and both conferences would be keen to maximize their slice.

Critics argue that such an arrangement could further entrench the dominance of the SEC and Big Ten, marginalizing smaller conferences that already struggle for exposure. The “Power Five” leagues have already benefited from the current system’s emphasis on conference championship games, and a joint scheduling pact could amplify that advantage. Smaller conferences may push for similar agreements among themselves, but without comparable financial clout, they risk being left out of the most lucrative time slots. Moreover, student‑athlete welfare concerns loom large; a longer season could increase injury risk and academic pressure, prompting the NCAA to revisit eligibility rules and player compensation models.

The upcoming years will be pivotal as conference leaders, the College Football Playoff Selection Committee, and the NCAA negotiate the logistics of a 24‑team format. While the exact details of any SEC‑Big Ten scheduling accord remain speculative, Klatt’s forecast underscores a broader trend toward greater collaboration among the sport’s elite. If the two powerhouses do align their calendars, the move could set a precedent for other conferences and reshape the college football landscape in ways that extend far beyond the gridiron.

Looking ahead, the 2027 season will serve as the first real test of the expanded playoff’s viability. Stakeholders will be watching closely to see whether the SEC and Big Ten can forge a mutually beneficial schedule that balances competitive integrity, financial gain, and player safety. Success could usher in a new era of cooperation among the nation’s top conferences, while failure might reignite calls for a more inclusive, decentralized postseason model. Either outcome will have lasting implications for the sport’s future, its fans, and the institutions that depend on its revenue.
